title: Stacks and queues
lesson:
Stacks and queues aren't new kinds of memory. They're **rules** about which item comes out next, built on the arrays and lists you already have.

**A stack: last in, first out.** Like a pile of plates: you add to the top and take from the top. Uses:
- **Undo** in a game or editor: push every move; undo pops the latest one.
- **Matching brackets** in code or a config file: push each opening bracket, pop when a closing one arrives.
- **Backtracking** in a maze or a robot path: push each step, pop to go back.
- Your program's own function calls run on "the call stack".

A dynamic array makes a perfect stack: **push** adds at `data[len]` (growing when full), **pop** takes `data[len - 1]`. Both ends of the work happen at the end of the array, so nothing ever shifts.

```
int stack_pop(Stack *s, int *out)
{
    if (s->len == 0) return 0;     /* empty: nothing to pop */
    *out = s->data[--s->len];
    return 1;
}
```

Notice the pattern from unit 1: the return value says *whether* it worked, and the out-parameter carries the value. Popping an empty stack is a normal situation, not a crash.

**A queue: first in, first out.** Like the line at a clinic desk: first to arrive is first served. Uses: game events, print jobs, patients, and bytes arriving over a serial cable.

**The ring buffer.** On a microcontroller, bytes arrive from the serial port (an interrupt puts them in), and the main loop takes them out when it's ready. Using malloc there is a bad idea, so the queue is a **fixed array used in a circle**:

```
typedef struct {
    unsigned char buf[8];
    int head;    /* next byte to read */
    int tail;    /* next place to write */
    int count;   /* bytes waiting */
} Ring;
```

- **put**: if `count == 8` it's full, refuse. Otherwise `buf[tail] = b; tail = (tail + 1) % 8; count++;`
- **get**: if `count == 0` it's empty. Otherwise `*out = buf[head]; head = (head + 1) % 8; count--;`

The `% 8` is the trick: after slot 7 comes slot 0 again, so the buffer never "runs out" as long as the reader keeps up. Keeping a `count` makes "full" and "empty" easy to tell apart, because `head == tail` happens in both cases.

**What if it's full?** Real firmware decides: drop the new byte (what we do here), or overwrite the oldest. Either way, never write past the array.

Arduino's `Serial` uses exactly this kind of ring buffer (64 bytes on an Uno). Audio, keyboards and network cards use them too.

notes: Queue q = {0}; starts empty: head, tail and count all 0.
put refuses when count == SIZE, so patient 5 is turned away.
tail = (tail + 1) % SIZE wraps from the last slot back to slot 0.
After serving patient 1, there's room again, and patient 6 goes into slot 0.
get returns 0 when empty, which is what ends the while loop: 2, 3, 4, 6.

exercises.title: Undo stack
exercises.prompt: Game moves are stored on a Stack (stack_init and stack_free given). Write int stack_push(Stack *s, int move): grow with my_realloc when full (4 when empty, then double; safe pattern), add move on top, return 1 (0 if memory runs out). Write int stack_pop(Stack *s, int *out): if empty return 0 and leave *out alone; otherwise store the top move in *out, remove it, return 1.

tests.call: ({ Stack s; stack_init(&s); stack_push(&s, 1); stack_push(&s, 2); stack_push(&s, 3); int a = 0, b = 0; stack_pop(&s, &a); stack_pop(&s, &b); stack_free(&s); a * 10 + b; })
tests.name: last in, first out

tests.call: ({ Stack s; stack_init(&s); int total = 0, v; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) stack_push(&s, i); while (stack_pop(&s, &v)) total += v; int r = total * 10 + s.len; stack_free(&s); r; })
tests.name: 100 moves in and out
tests.hint_if_fail: Grow the array when len == cap.

tests.call: ({ Stack s; stack_init(&s); int v = -1; int ok = stack_pop(&s, &v); stack_free(&s); ok * 100 + v; })
tests.name: pop when empty

tests.call: ({ Stack s; stack_init(&s); stack_push(&s, 1); stack_push(&s, 2); int a = 0, b = 0, c = 0; stack_pop(&s, &a); stack_push(&s, 5); stack_pop(&s, &b); stack_pop(&s, &c); stack_free(&s); a * 100 + b * 10 + c; })
tests.name: pop, push, pop

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; Stack s; stack_init(&s); for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) stack_push(&s, i); int r = (live_allocs - before) * 100 + s.cap; stack_free(&s); r; })
tests.name: one block, capacity 64

hints: stack_push is list_push from unit 4 with new names.

exercises.title: Bracket checker
exercises.prompt: A robot reads settings like {"arm": [1, (2)]}. Write int brackets_ok(const char *s): return 1 if every (, [ and { is closed by the matching ), ] or } in the right order, else 0. Other characters are ignored; an empty string is fine. Use a stack (a heap char array from my_alloc is enough: there can't be more open brackets than characters) and free it before returning.

tests.name: wrong closer
tests.hint_if_fail: A closer must match the most recent opener: that's the top of the stack.

tests.name: never closed
tests.hint_if_fail: At the end, the stack must be empty.

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; brackets_ok("([{}])"); brackets_ok("(("); live_allocs - before; })
tests.name: frees its stack

hints: If strlen(s) is 0, return 1. Otherwise char *stack = my_alloc(strlen(s)); and an int top = 0.
An opener: stack[top++] = c. A closer: if top == 0 or stack[top - 1] isn't its partner, it's bad; otherwise top--.
At the end the answer is ok && top == 0. my_free(stack) before every return.

exercises.title: Serial ring buffer
exercises.prompt: Bytes arrive from a serial port faster than the main loop reads them. With the Ring type given (RING_SIZE 8, start with Ring r = {0};), write int ring_put(Ring *r, unsigned char b): if full return 0 and change nothing; otherwise store b at tail, move tail on (wrapping to 0 after the last slot), add 1 to count, return 1. Write int ring_get(Ring *r, unsigned char *out): if empty return 0; otherwise give back the byte at head, move head on (wrapping), subtract 1 from count, return 1.

tests.call: ({ Ring r = {0}; ring_put(&r, 'A'); ring_put(&r, 'B'); unsigned char x = 0, y = 0; ring_get(&r, &x); ring_get(&r, &y); x * 1000 + y; })
tests.name: first in, first out

tests.call: ({ Ring r = {0}; int ok = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) ok += ring_put(&r, i); ok * 10 + ring_put(&r, 99); })
tests.name: holds 8, refuses the 9th

tests.call: ({ Ring r = {0}; unsigned char v = 7; int ok = ring_get(&r, &v); ok * 100 + v; })
tests.name: empty gives nothing

tests.call: ({ Ring r = {0}; unsigned char v; for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) ring_put(&r, i); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) ring_get(&r, &v); for (int i = 10; i < 15; i++) ring_put(&r, i); int s = 0; while (ring_get(&r, &v)) s = s * 100 + v; s; })
tests.name: wraps around the end
tests.hint_if_fail: tail = (tail + 1) % RING_SIZE; and the same for head.

tests.call: ({ Ring r = {0}; unsigned char v; for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { ring_put(&r, i); ring_put(&r, i); ring_get(&r, &v); ring_get(&r, &v); } r.count * 100 + (r.head == r.tail) * 10 + (r.head < RING_SIZE); })
tests.name: stays in bounds after many laps

tests.call: ({ Ring r = {0}; unsigned char v; for (int i = 0; i < 9; i++) ring_put(&r, i); ring_get(&r, &v); int a = v; ring_put(&r, 50); for (int i = 0; i < 7; i++) ring_get(&r, &v); ring_get(&r, &v); a * 100 + v; })
tests.name: full ring drops the new byte

hints: ring_get mirrors it with head: *out = r->buf[r->head]; ...

quiz.q: You push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack and pop once. What comes out?
Patients 1, 2, 3 join a queue. Who is served first?
Why keep a count in a ring buffer?
choices: head == tail happens both when empty and when full; count tells them apart
quiz.why: count says which case you're in.

quiz.q: Why is a ring buffer popular on microcontrollers?
choices: Fixed memory, no malloc, and it never shifts items
quiz.why: A fixed array used in a circle.

quiz.q: Which job fits a stack best?
choices: Undoing the last move in a game
quiz.why: Undo takes back the most recent thing first.

cards.a: Last in, first out (push and pop at the top).

cards.q: Move an index round a ring of size N?

explain: Explain how a ring buffer reuses its slots, walking through a small example with 4 slots and some bytes you choose.
